SCHOOL GARDEN · GARDEN FRIENDS

Garden Animals & Friends

Age 2 YearsSubject Nature & TalkClass School GardenDuration 3–5 minutes

A bird in the hedge, a worm after the rain, an owl you might only hear — meet the animals that live around gardens and the great outdoors, one big picture at a time.

Nothing to prepare and nothing to read to your toddler. You say the name, they point or hop — a moment on a card counts, and the real outdoors can wait for your next walk.

Start the Class ↓Start with the bird — the easiest friend to spot from a window.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Ten little steps, in order: a welcome from your teacher, all eighteen garden friends, two gentle games, a look-don’t-touch outdoors hunt, cards to print, a note from your teacher and one last check-in from you. Stop after any step — that is a complete class.

LEARN · MEET THE GARDEN FRIENDS

Meet the garden friends.

Eighteen big picture cards, one at a time. Say the name clearly, make the sound together, and let your toddler point, giggle or move along.

PLAY · FIND THE ANIMAL

Find the animal.

Three big pictures, one question. You say the animal, your child taps it — a wrong tap simply means look together.

Find the bird.

Where’s the frog?

Find the rabbit.

Can you find the squirrel?

Where’s the owl?

PLAY · WHO AM I?

Who am I?

A little clue, then three friends. Say the clue slowly and let your child solve it — every guess is a good guess.

I have long ears. Who am I?

I hop. Who am I?

I have a bushy tail. Who am I?

I fly at night. Who am I?

I say quack. Who am I?

I have a shell. Who am I?

TOGETHER · WHERE MIGHT WE SEE IT?

Where might we see it?

Some of these friends live in gardens, some just visit, and some live in the wider outdoors — here is where to look, gently and from a distance.

  • Bird

    “Hedges, parks and balconies — you will hear one before you see it.”

  • Squirrel

    “Up in the trees of any leafy park, tail twitching.”

  • Duck

    “On ponds and canals, paddling along in a little line.”

  • Rabbit

    “At the edges of meadows and gardens, early in the morning.”

  • Frog

    “Near ponds, puddles and damp grass, especially after rain.”

  • Worm

    “In the soil and under flowerpots after it rains — look, then leave them be.”

  • Hedgehog

    “In hedges and leaf piles after dark, if you are lucky.”

  • Bat

    “Flitting through the evening sky just after sunset.”

  • Owl

    “High in old trees at night — usually a whooo long before a look.”

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

A look-don’t-touch nature hunt.

Take the names outside — or to a window, a book or a video if the outdoors is far away. Wild animals are looked at, never touched, chased or fed.

Try one today

  • Spot a bird from the window and say its name together.
  • Watch a squirrel’s tail twitch in the park.
  • After rain, look for a worm on the path — look with your eyes, then walk on by.
  • At dusk, look up and search for bats — pointing and whispering is plenty.
  • Hop like a frog and wiggle like a worm yourselves — the safest animals to touch are you two.

Never feed wild animals, never touch or pick up an unknown animal, and never follow one for a closer look. A grown-up stays close the whole time — one spotted friend is a complete hunt.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Your toddler does not need every animal name to stick. Saying words while they look and hop is the whole lesson — the vocabulary rides along, and no garden is required. Some of these friends live in gardens, some only visit, and some live in the wider outdoors — all of that is fine to wonder about together.

More from the Principal’s Office ↗

CLASS COMPLETE

Class complete!

From the twitchy squirrel to the owl you may only ever hear — what a little tour of the outdoors. However many rounds you played, however long it took, that was the whole class — and stopping early is allowed too.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

Follow your toddler’s favourites. If the frog gets five rounds in a row, the frog gets five rounds in a row — repetition is how little ones learn.

Sounds and movement before facts. Hopping, wiggling and quacking teach the names better than any explanation, so be as silly as your toddler needs you to be.

Keep it honest and gentle: some of these animals live in gardens, some just visit and some stay far outdoors — and all of them stay wild. Looking is the game; touching, feeding and chasing are not part of it.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.
